62775.q: Roughly how long is the Great Aletsch Glacier, the longest glacier in the Alps?
62775.e: The Great Aletsch Glacier is around 20 km long, making it the longest glacier in the Alps. It is the heart of the Jungfrau-Aletsch World Heritage Site but is shrinking considerably because of global warming.
62775.m: At around 20 kilometres, the Aletsch Glacier is the longest glacier in the Alps.

62776.q: Which ecological process can be observed especially well in front of the retreating tongue of the Aletsch Glacier?
62776.e: On the newly exposed glacier ground, pioneer plants settle first, followed later by shrubs and forest. This sequence on raw soil is called primary succession.
62776.m: In the glacier forefield, life begins with primary succession.

62777.q: Which major geological unit does most of the Jungfrau-Aletsch World Heritage Site belong to?
62777.e: The Aar Massif consists mainly of crystalline rocks such as granite and gneiss. On its northern edge are limestones, some of which were pushed over the crystalline rock.
62777.m: Most of the Jungfrau-Aletsch World Heritage Site lies in the Aar Massif.

62778.q: What is the large firn basin called where several ice streams join to form the Great Aletsch Glacier?
62778.e: At the Konkordiaplatz, several firn streams meet and form the Great Aletsch Glacier. The ice there is several hundred metres thick.
62778.m: At the Konkordiaplatz, the ice streams of the Aletsch Glacier meet.

62779.q: In which Valais town is the World Nature Forum visitor centre of the Jungfrau-Aletsch World Heritage Site?
62779.e: The World Nature Forum in Naters informs visitors about glaciers, nature and culture in the World Heritage Site. Naters is near Brig at the foot of the Aletsch area.
62779.m: The World Nature Forum of the World Heritage Site is in Naters.

62780.q: What change did the Monte San Giorgio World Heritage Site undergo in 2010?
a: Extension to include the Italian part
62780.e: In 2010, the southern part of the mountain, which belongs to Italy, was added. Since then Monte San Giorgio has been a cross-border World Heritage Site.
62780.m: Since 2010 Monte San Giorgio has been a joint World Heritage Site with Italy.

62781.q: In which rock are many of the famous fossils of Monte San Giorgio enclosed?
62781.e: Many finds come from dark, bitumen-rich shale layers of the Triassic. These shales were once even mined to extract oil.
62781.m: The fossils of Monte San Giorgio are often found in bitumen-rich shale.

62782.q: How many whole municipalities belong to the UNESCO Biosphere Entlebuch?
62782.e: The biosphere covers seven municipalities in the canton of Lucerne and the village of Schachen in the municipality of Werthenstein. Together they form an association of municipalities.
62782.m: Seven municipalities support the UNESCO Biosphere Entlebuch.

62783.q: How was the founding of the Entlebuch Biosphere decided?
a: In votes by the local people
62783.e: The people of the Entlebuch voted on the project themselves. The biosphere was therefore created through direct democracy.
62783.m: The people of the Entlebuch decided on their biosphere themselves.

62784.q: Which federal vote gave rise to the idea of a biosphere in the Entlebuch?
62784.e: Moorland protection put large parts of the Entlebuch under protection, which was first felt to be a restriction. The region turned this into an opportunity and became a model region for protection and use.
62784.m: Moorland protection led to the idea of a biosphere in the Entlebuch.

62785.q: Which nature discovery park lies in the forests above Lausanne?
62785.e: In the Jorat north-east of Lausanne, the forest in the core zone is left to itself. It is one of two nature discovery parks in Switzerland.
62785.m: The Jorat near Lausanne is a nature discovery park.

62786.q: Which project for a national park in Ticino was rejected by the municipalities in 2018?
62786.e: The project covered areas around the Centovalli, Onsernone and Brissago. Several municipalities voted against it in 2018.
62786.m: The Parco Nazionale del Locarnese failed in 2018 because of the municipalities.

62787.q: Which two zones must a new national park have under the Parks Ordinance?
62787.e: In the core zone, nature is left to itself. The buffer zone is for near-natural use and protects the core zone from outside influences.
62787.m: A national park consists of a core zone and a buffer zone.

62788.q: Why is it difficult to create a new national park in Switzerland?
a: It needs a very large core zone with no use
The law allows only one national park
National parks may only be in the Jura
National parks must be on a national border
62788.e: In the Alps, the core zone must be at least 100 km². Hunting, logging and much more are forbidden there, which often meets with resistance.
62788.m: New national parks need large core zones with no use.

62789.q: Which regional nature park also includes municipalities in Germany?
62789.e: The Schaffhausen Regional Nature Park is cross-border and also includes neighbouring German municipalities. It is shaped by vineyards, forests and farmland.
62789.m: The Schaffhausen Nature Park reaches across the border into Germany.

62790.q: Roughly how large is the vineyard area in the Lavaux World Heritage Site?
62790.e: The World Heritage Site covers over 805 ha of vineyards. Some of the terraces are very steep and narrow.
62790.m: Lavaux covers over 800 hectares of vines.

62791.q: Which “three suns” are said to warm the vines in Lavaux?
a: Sun, reflection from the lake and warm walls
62791.e: The vines receive direct sunlight, light reflected from Lake Geneva and the heat stored by the stone walls. That is why the grapes ripen so well there.
62791.m: In Lavaux, sun, lake and walls warm the vines.

62792.q: How did the voters of Vaud decide on the protection of Lavaux in May 2014?
62792.e: Around 70 per cent rejected the stricter initiative, and around 73 per cent accepted the moderate counter-proposal. The protection was thus laid down in a law.
62792.m: In 2014 the counter-proposal won in Lavaux.

62793.q: As what kind of World Heritage is Lavaux listed?
62793.e: Lavaux shows how people have shaped a landscape over centuries. That is why it counts as a cultural landscape and not as natural heritage.
62793.m: Lavaux is World Heritage as a cultural landscape.

62794.q: Which animal was discovered as a new species in the Hölloch in 2010?
62794.e: In 2010, the pseudoscorpion Pseudoblothrus infernus was described. It is adapted to life in complete darkness.
62794.m: A pseudoscorpion of its own lives in the Hölloch.

62795.q: Which hoofed animals are often seen on the cliffs of the Creux du Van?
62795.e: Ibex and chamois are skilful climbers and find shelter on the rock ledges. They can often be watched from close by.
62795.m: Ibex and chamois climb in the Creux du Van.

62796.q: Above which valley is the Creux du Van?
62796.e: The rock basin lies above the Val de Travers, near the border with the canton of Vaud. A steep path leads up from Noiraigue.
62796.m: The Creux du Van lies above the Val de Travers.

62797.q: Which shrub often forms dense thickets above the forest line on damp, shady slopes?
62797.e: The green alder, also called alpine alder, grows on damp steep slopes and in avalanche tracks. It spreads strongly on abandoned alpine pastures.
62797.m: The green alder forms dense thickets above the forest line.

62798.q: What did every BLN site receive when the inventory was revised in 2017?
62798.e: In the 2017 revision, each site was given a precise description and specific protection goals. There is no general building ban in the BLN.
62798.m: Since 2017 every BLN site has specific protection goals.

62799.q: In contrast to rich meadows, what are unfertilised, species-rich meadows generally called?
62799.e: Nutrient-poor meadows receive little or no fertiliser and are therefore low in nutrients and rich in species. Dry meadows are an especially dry form of them.
62799.m: Unfertilised, species-rich meadows are called nutrient-poor meadows.

62800.q: What role do intact moors play for the climate?
a: They store large amounts of carbon
They produce a lot of ozone
They take nitrogen from the air
62800.e: Because dead plants hardly decompose in wet peat, their carbon stays stored. If moors are drained, it escapes as CO2.
62800.m: Intact moors are important carbon stores.

62801.q: Who organised a group trip by train from Leicester to Loughborough in 1841, which is considered the beginning of organised tourism?
62801.e: The English Baptist preacher Thomas Cook organised a special trip for about 500 members of a temperance movement in 1841. This grew into one of the first travel companies in the world.
62801.m: With his 1841 train trip, Thomas Cook is seen as the pioneer of the package holiday.

62802.q: Which Swiss tourism researcher criticised the effects of mass tourism in the Alps in his 1975 book “Die Landschaftsfresser” (The Landscape Eaters)?
62802.e: Jost Krippendorf, a professor at the University of Bern, warned early on about urban sprawl and the consumption of landscape by tourism. He is considered a pioneer of soft tourism.
62802.m: With “The Landscape Eaters” Jost Krippendorf denounced the consumption of landscape by tourism.

62803.q: What does the leakage rate describe in tourism?
a: The share of tourism income that flows abroad
The share of guests who never come back
The loss of water in hotel complexes
The share of empty hotel beds
62803.e: Income flows out again, for example through imported food, foreign hotel chains or tour operators. In many developing countries only a small share stays in the country.
62803.m: A high leakage rate means that little tourism money stays in the holiday country.

a: At least two travel services for one total price
A trip without a fixed return date
A trip only in your own car
62804.e: In a package holiday, a tour operator bundles flights and hotel, for example, into one package at a total price. From the 1960s it made holidays abroad affordable for broad sections of the population.
62804.m: A package holiday sells transport and accommodation as one package.

62805.q: Which means of transport made package holidays to the Mediterranean affordable for broad sections of the population from the 1960s?
a: The long-distance coach with reclining seats
62805.e: Charter airlines flew full planes directly to holiday destinations such as Majorca or the Canary Islands. Together with rising incomes and paid holidays, this created mass tourism.
62805.m: Charter flights were a driving force of mass tourism in the Mediterranean.

62806.e: The term describes the classic beach holiday on warm coasts. It shapes mass tourism, for example on the Spanish Mediterranean coast.
62806.m: 3S tourism relies on sun, sea and sand.

62807.q: What is meant by enclave tourism?
a: Closed-off holiday resorts with little contact with the local population
Trips to small states such as San Marino
62807.e: Guests stay in fenced all-inclusive resorts and spend hardly any money outside. As a result, the local economy benefits little.
62807.m: Enclave tourism separates guests from the local population.

62808.q: Which town on the Spanish Costa Blanca, with its many high-rise hotels, is considered a symbol of mass tourism?
62808.e: From the 1950s Benidorm changed from a fishing village into a high-rise town with a very large number of hotel beds. The dense building saves space but strongly shapes the coast.
62808.m: Benidorm is a well-known example of vertical mass tourism.

62809.q: What did Venice introduce in April 2024 as a measure against overtourism?
a: An entry fee for day visitors
62809.e: On selected peak days, day visitors who do not stay overnight have to pay a fee. In this way the city wants to manage the flow of visitors.
62809.m: On peak days Venice charges day tourists a fee.

62810.q: Who does not have to pay the entry fee in Venice?
a: Guests who stay overnight in the city
62810.e: Anyone staying overnight in Venice already pays a tourist tax and is exempt. Day visitors pay 5 euros on peak days, and since 2025 those who book at the last minute pay 10 euros.
62810.m: Venice's fee affects day tourists, not overnight guests.

62811.q: Below which mark did the number of inhabitants of Venice's historic old town fall in 2022?
62811.e: In the 1950s about 175,000 people still lived in the old town. High rents, holiday flats and the change into a tourist city drove many to the mainland.
62811.m: Venice's old town now has fewer than 50,000 inhabitants.

62812.q: Which ships have been banned from passing through the Giudecca Canal and the St Mark's Basin in Venice since 2021?
62812.e: In 2021 the Italian government banned ships over 25,000 gross tonnage from the historic centre. The reasons were waves, exhaust fumes and the risk of accidents.
62812.m: Large cruise ships may no longer sail past St Mark's Square in Venice.

62813.q: What does the term overtourism mean?
a: Tourism that exceeds the limits a place can bear
Trips with more than one overnight stay
62813.e: With overtourism, the quality of life of local people and the experience of guests suffer from too many visitors. Overcrowding, rising rents and protests are typical.
62813.m: Overtourism happens when a place has more guests than it can cope with.

62814.q: According to the Irridex model, how does the attitude of local people change as more and more tourists come?
62814.e: In 1975 George Doxey described a development from euphoria through apathy and annoyance to antagonism. As the number of tourists grows, the hostility grows.
62814.m: In the Irridex, local hostility rises to open antagonism.

62815.q: Which city wants to let all its roughly 10,000 licences for tourist holiday flats expire by 2028?
62815.e: Barcelona announced this in 2024 in order to win back housing for local people. In the same year residents there protested against overtourism with water pistols.
62815.m: Barcelona is taking action against holiday flats to protect housing.

62816.q: What do you call the displacement of residents when flats and shops in a neighbourhood are increasingly geared towards tourists?
62816.e: Holiday flats and souvenir shops replace rented flats and local shops. The term is modelled on gentrification.
62816.m: Touristification pushes local people out of popular districts.

62817.q: Which list did UNESCO recommend putting Venice on in 2023, which the World Heritage Committee then rejected?
a: List of World Heritage in Danger
62817.e: Expert bodies saw Venice as threatened by mass tourism, climate change and building projects. In September 2023 the World Heritage Committee decided not to add it.
62817.m: In 2023 Venice narrowly escaped being put on the List of World Heritage in Danger.

62818.q: According to the industry association CLIA, how many passengers went on an ocean cruise worldwide in 2024?
62818.e: CLIA reported a record of about 34.6 million ocean passengers for 2024. That was well above the 2019 figure before the pandemic.
62818.m: Cruises reached a record of about 35 million guests in 2024.

62819.q: Which ship was the largest cruise ship in the world when it entered service in 2024?
62819.e: The Icon of the Seas of the Royal Caribbean line is about 365 metres long and has room for more than 7000 passengers. Critics see such ships as a symbol of mass tourism at sea.
62819.m: The Icon of the Seas set a new size record in 2024.

62820.q: What is the purpose of shore power facilities in cruise ports?
a: Ships take electricity from the land and switch off their engines
Ships load drinking water on land
Passengers charge their mobile phones for free
Ports light up the berths at night
62820.e: Without shore power, the diesel generators keep running in port and pollute the city's air. With shore power, exhaust fumes and noise at the berth fall.
62820.m: Shore power reduces the exhaust fumes of cruise ships in port.

62821.q: Why are many cruise ships registered in countries such as Panama, the Bahamas or Malta?
a: Because of lower taxes and looser rules
Because only shipyards there build ships
Because these flags scare off pirates
62821.e: These are called flags of convenience. Shipping companies save on taxes and costs, for example in employment law.
62821.m: Flags of convenience lower the costs of shipping companies.

62822.q: Why do port cities often benefit little from cruise guests?
a: The guests mostly sleep and eat on board
The guests may not leave the ship
The ships only dock at night
The guests pay no port fees
62822.e: Cruise guests often stay on land for only a few hours and spend little on accommodation and restaurants. At the same time they put a heavy strain on old towns.
62822.m: Cruise guests bring big crowds but little income on land.

62823.q: Which sea region is the most important cruising area in the world?
62823.e: The Caribbean is close to the large North American market and has warm weather all year round. Florida, with Miami, is an important departure port.
62823.m: The Caribbean is the largest cruising area in the world.

62824.q: Which fuel is often used on new cruise ships as a lower-pollution alternative to heavy fuel oil?
62824.e: Liquefied natural gas produces much less sulphur and soot than heavy fuel oil. However, methane slip is criticised, because methane is a strong greenhouse gas.
62824.m: LNG reduces pollutants but is still a fossil fuel.

62825.q: Why may only small groups of cruise guests go ashore at the same time in Antarctica?
a: To protect animals and fragile nature
Because the harbours there are too small
Because there is no electricity on land
62825.e: The association of Antarctic tour operators, IAATO, allows a maximum of 100 people at a landing site at the same time. Ships with more than 500 passengers may not make any landings at all.
62825.m: Strict rules protect Antarctica's nature from too many visitors.

a: Travel into nature that protects it and benefits the local population
Cheap package holidays in large beach hotels
Holidays on a farm in Switzerland
62826.e: The term was coined in the 1980s. Ecotourism is meant to fund nature conservation and give local people an income.
62826.m: Ecotourism combines nature experiences, conservation and local income.

62827.q: Roughly what share of Costa Rica's land area is protected, for example as a national park or reserve?
62827.e: Costa Rica has a dense network of national parks, reserves and protected areas. This nature is the basis of its ecotourism.
62827.m: About a quarter of Costa Rica is protected.

62828.q: Roughly what share of the world's biodiversity is found in Costa Rica, even though the country makes up only about 0.03 per cent of the Earth's land area?
62828.e: Costa Rica lies between two oceans and has many climate and altitude zones. That is why it is one of the most species-rich countries on Earth.
62828.m: Costa Rica is home to about five per cent of all species on a tiny area.

62829.q: Why does ecotourism need independent sustainability certificates?
a: So that travellers can tell genuine offers from greenwashing
So that hotels pay higher taxes
So that only local people may travel
62829.e: Many providers call themselves “eco” without doing much for the environment. Costa Rica therefore rates businesses with the CST certificate according to ecological and social criteria.
62829.m: Certificates help you recognise genuine ecotourism.

62830.q: What has Costa Rica been paying landowners for since 1997 in the programme “Pago por Servicios Ambientales”?
62830.e: Forests store CO2 and protect water and biodiversity. The programme is funded partly by a fuel tax.
62830.m: Costa Rica pays landowners to preserve forest.

62831.q: How has Costa Rica's forest area developed since the 1980s?
a: It rose from about a fifth to over half of the country's area
It fell from half to a tenth
It stayed constant at a third
62831.e: After heavy clearing for pasture, the forest recovered thanks to protected areas and payments for environmental services. Ecotourism also created an extra incentive to preserve forest.
62831.m: Costa Rica has more than doubled its forest area since the 1980s.

62832.q: Which type of forest makes the Monteverde reserve in Costa Rica a well-known ecotourism destination?
62832.e: In Monteverde clouds drift through the mountain forest almost constantly and provide moisture. Visitors come for the orchids, quetzals and suspension bridges.
62832.m: Monteverde is famous for its cloud forest.

62833.q: Which animals do ecotourists particularly watch in Tortuguero National Park on Costa Rica's Caribbean coast?
62833.e: Tortuguero means roughly “place of the turtles”. Night tours are strictly regulated so that the animals are not disturbed.
62833.m: Tortuguero is an important nesting site for sea turtles.

62834.q: Roughly how high above sea level is the highest natural point of the Maldives?
62834.e: The Maldives are the flattest country in the world. A rising sea level therefore threatens islands, resorts and drinking water.
62834.m: The Maldives rise hardly more than two metres out of the sea.

62835.q: Which principle shapes resort tourism in the Maldives?
a: Every island open to all guests
62835.e: Each resort usually occupies its own otherwise uninhabited island. This keeps tourists and the local population largely separate.
62835.m: In the Maldives each resort usually has its own island.

62836.q: In which decade did the first holiday resorts open in the Maldives?
62836.e: In 1972 the first resort, Kurumba, opened with just a few rooms. Since then tourism has become the most important branch of the economy.
62836.m: Resort tourism in the Maldives began in 1972.

62837.q: Where may tourists legally drink alcohol in the Maldives?
a: On resort islands and hotel boats
62837.e: The Maldives are an Islamic state, and alcohol is banned on inhabited islands. Resorts and safari boats receive special permits.
62837.m: In the Maldives alcohol is only available in resorts and on hotel boats.

62838.q: How did the Maldivian president Mohamed Nasheed draw attention to climate change in 2009?
a: With a cabinet meeting under water
With a hunger strike in New York
62838.e: The ministers dived in scuba gear and signed an appeal to reduce CO2. The event showed the threat from the rising sea level.
62838.m: In 2009 the Maldives held a cabinet meeting under water.

62839.q: What is the name of the artificially built-up island next to Malé that lies higher than natural islands and is meant to create living space?
62839.e: Hulhumalé was built up from coral sand from 1997 and lies about two metres above the sea. It relieves the overcrowded capital and serves as an adaptation to climate change.
62839.m: Hulhumalé is an artificial island in response to lack of space and rising sea levels.

62840.q: What causes the coral bleaching that threatens the reefs and therefore diving tourism in the Maldives?
a: Sea temperatures that are too high
62840.e: Under heat stress, corals expel their colourful algae and turn white. If the heat lasts, they die, as in the events of 1998 and 2016.
62840.m: Heat stress in the sea bleaches corals.

62841.q: Which form of accommodation has been newly allowed in the Maldives since rules were relaxed around 2009?
a: Houseboats in the lagoon of Malé
62841.e: Before that, tourists were allowed almost only on resort islands. Guesthouses bring local people more direct income and offer cheaper holidays.
62841.m: Guesthouses open the local islands of the Maldives to tourism.

62842.q: According to a common rule of thumb, when is a ski area considered snow-reliable?
a: With at least 100 snow days per season
With at least 30 snow days per season
With at least 60 snow days per season
With at least 150 snow days per season
62842.e: According to this rule of thumb, a ski area needs enough snow cover on at least 100 days in seven out of ten winters. Otherwise it is considered economically at risk.
62842.m: A ski area is snow-reliable with at least a hundred snow days per season.

62843.q: By roughly how much does the snow line rise for each degree Celsius of warming?
62843.e: Warmer air makes precipitation fall as rain more often. Lower ski areas are therefore the first to lose their snow reliability.
62843.m: For every degree of warming the snow line rises by about 150 metres.

62844.q: By roughly how much has Switzerland warmed since pre-industrial times (as of 2024)?
62844.e: According to MeteoSwiss, warming in Switzerland is about 2.9 °C. That is about twice as much as the global average.
62844.m: Switzerland is warming about twice as fast as the global average.

62845.q: Which weather conditions are best for making artificial snow?
62845.e: The water droplets have to freeze in the air. Dry air cools them further through evaporation, which is why the so-called wet-bulb temperature matters.
62845.m: Artificial snow works best in cold, dry air.

62846.q: What is meant by snow farming?
a: Storing snow over the summer under wood chips
Bringing snow from abroad by lorry
Making snow chemically from salt water
Using snow as feed for farm animals
62846.e: Large heaps of snow are insulated with wood chips or sheets. This way only part of the snow is lost, and a cross-country trail or piste can be prepared early in autumn.
62846.m: In snow farming, snow is preserved over the summer.

62847.q: Which ski areas are considered most at risk from climate change?
a: Low-lying ski areas in the Prealps and the Jura
Ski areas on north-facing slopes above 2500 metres
High alpine ski areas in Valais
62847.e: The lower a ski area lies, the more often rain falls instead of snow and the more expensive artificial snow becomes. In Switzerland several small low-lying ski areas have already been abandoned.
62847.m: Low-lying ski areas are the first to lose their snow reliability.

62848.q: In which Swiss resort is the largest summer ski area in the Alps?
62848.e: On the Theodul Glacier near the Klein Matterhorn you can ski even in summer. Because the glacier is melting, however, the area is shrinking.
62848.m: Zermatt offers skiing on the glacier even in summer.

62849.q: Which strategy do many mountain resorts follow to depend less on winter sports?
a: Closing all mountain railways in summer
Moving the pistes to the lowlands
62849.e: Activities such as hiking, mountain biking, culture and wellness spread the income over the whole year. This is also called four-season tourism.
62849.m: Year-round tourism makes mountain resorts less dependent on snow.

62850.q: Who published the model of the Tourism Area Life Cycle in 1980?
62850.e: The geographer Richard Butler described how tourist places go through typical stages of development. The model is one of the most cited in tourism geography.
62850.m: Richard Butler developed the life cycle of tourist destinations in 1980.

62851.q: Which economic model is Butler's Tourism Area Life Cycle based on?
62851.e: Like a product, a destination goes through introduction, growth, maturity and decline. Butler applied this idea to holiday resorts.
62851.m: Butler applied the product life cycle to holiday resorts.

62852.q: What is the first stage in Butler's Tourism Area Life Cycle called?
62852.e: In the exploration stage only a few adventurous travellers come. There is hardly any tourist infrastructure.
62852.m: At the beginning of the life cycle, a few pioneers discover a destination.

62853.q: In which stage according to Butler do local people begin to offer the first accommodation and services for guests?
62853.e: In the involvement stage a simple local offer develops and a season takes shape. Control is still largely in the hands of local people.
62853.m: In the involvement stage local people enter the tourism business.

62854.q: What is typical of the development stage according to Butler?
a: Outside investors and hotel chains increasingly take control
62854.e: Visitor numbers grow quickly and large complexes are built. Local influence decreases, and the look of the place changes greatly.
62854.m: In the development stage outside investors often take over the business.

62855.q: Which stage follows the development stage in Butler's model?
62855.e: In consolidation, visitor numbers grow only slowly and tourism dominates the economy. After that, stagnation threatens.
62855.m: Development is followed by consolidation with slower growth.

62856.q: What characterises the stagnation stage in the Tourism Area Life Cycle?
a: Capacity limits are reached and the image seems outdated
The first tourists discover the place
Local people open the first guesthouses
62856.e: The limits of what the place can bear are reached, and environmental and social problems increase. The place lives mainly from regular guests.
62856.m: In stagnation a destination reaches its limits.

62857.q: Which two basic developments are possible after stagnation according to Butler?
62857.e: Without new ideas the destination loses guests and falls into decay. With renewal, such as new attractions or target groups, it can be rejuvenated.
62857.m: After stagnation, renewal decides between decline and rejuvenation.

62858.q: Which US coastal city did Butler give as an example of rejuvenation through allowing casinos?
62858.e: The seaside resort of Atlantic City on the New Jersey coast had lost its appeal. From 1976 casinos were allowed in order to revive the town.
62858.m: Atlantic City tried to rejuvenate itself with casinos.

62859.q: In which month of the Islamic calendar does the Hajj to Mecca take place?
62859.e: The Hajj is one of the five pillars of Islam and takes place every year in the twelfth month of the lunar calendar. Because the lunar year is shorter, the date moves every year.
62859.m: The Hajj takes place in the pilgrimage month of Dhu al-Hijjah.

62860.q: What is the smaller pilgrimage to Mecca called which, unlike the Hajj, can be made all year round?
62860.e: The Umrah is voluntary and not tied to a fixed date. Saudi Arabia actively promotes it as part of its tourism strategy.
62860.m: Unlike the Hajj, the Umrah can be made at any time.

62861.q: What minimum distance must you walk to receive the pilgrim certificate “Compostela” in Santiago de Compostela?
62861.e: Walking pilgrims must cover at least the last 100 kilometres, cycling pilgrims at least 200 kilometres. The stages are proven with stamps in the pilgrim passport.
62861.m: For the Compostela you must walk at least a hundred kilometres.

62862.q: When is there a Holy Year (Año Santo Xacobeo) in Santiago de Compostela?
a: When 25 July falls on a Sunday
When a new pope is elected
62862.e: 25 July is the feast day of the apostle James. In Holy Years the number of pilgrims rises sharply.
62862.m: A Holy Year of St James is when St James' Day falls on a Sunday.

62863.q: Roughly how many pilgrims received a pilgrim certificate in Santiago de Compostela in 2024?
62863.e: In 2024 the pilgrims' office registered just under 500,000 pilgrims, more than ever before. The Way of St James is therefore also an important tourism product.
62863.m: The Way of St James attracts about half a million pilgrims a year.

62864.q: Which Swiss place of pilgrimage, with its Benedictine monastery and Black Madonna, is the most important in the country?
62864.e: Einsiedeln in the canton of Schwyz has attracted pilgrims since the Middle Ages. The town also lies on the Swiss Way of St James.
62864.m: Einsiedeln is the most important place of pilgrimage in Switzerland.

62865.q: In which city does the Swiss Way of St James (ViaJacobi) leave Switzerland towards France?
62865.e: The ViaJacobi runs from Lake Constance via Einsiedeln, Schwyz, the Brünig Pass, Fribourg and Lausanne to Geneva. From there it continues in France on the Via Gebennensis towards Le Puy and Spain.
62865.m: The Swiss Way of St James ends in Geneva.

62866.q: In which year is Bernadette Soubirous said to have seen visions of the Virgin Mary in Lourdes?
62866.e: Since the visions of 1858, Lourdes has developed into one of the largest places of pilgrimage in the world. Many sick people travel there hoping to be healed.
62866.m: Lourdes became a place of pilgrimage after the visions of Mary in 1858.

62867.q: At the confluence of which rivers did the Kumbh Mela, one of the largest religious festivals in the world, take place in Prayagraj in 2025?
62867.e: Devout Hindus bathe at this confluence to cleanse themselves of sins. According to Indian authorities, several hundred million people came.
62867.m: The Kumbh Mela of Prayagraj takes place at the confluence of the Ganges and Yamuna.

62868.q: What does the abbreviation MICE stand for in city tourism?
62868.e: MICE refers to business travel and conference tourism. It brings cities such as Zurich, Geneva or Basel many overnight stays during the week.
62868.m: MICE covers meetings, incentive trips, conventions and trade fairs.

62869.q: What is the charge called that guests pay in addition for each night in many Swiss municipalities?
62869.e: With the tourist tax, municipalities fund services for guests, such as guest cards or events. Other cities around the world charge a so-called city tax.
62869.m: Guests pay the tourist tax to the municipality for each night.

62870.q: Which city decided in 2024 not to approve any new hotels and wants to limit overnight stays to 20 million a year?
62870.e: Amsterdam suffers from overtourism in its old town. A new hotel may only open if another one closes.
62870.m: Amsterdam slows down tourism with a hotel freeze.

62871.q: Which museum is considered the most visited in the world?
a: The Metropolitan Museum in New York
62871.e: The Louvre counts about eight to nine million visits a year. The Mona Lisa is the biggest crowd puller.
62871.m: The Louvre is the most visited museum in the world.

62872.q: Which Swiss city records the most hotel overnight stays?
62872.e: In the statistics of the Federal Statistical Office, Zurich regularly comes ahead of Geneva and Basel. Business trips and city breaks contribute to this.
62872.m: Zurich is the Swiss city with the most hotel overnight stays.

62873.q: Which city was the first European Capital of Culture in 1985?
62873.e: The idea came from the Greek culture minister Melina Mercouri. The title often gives cities a clear boost in cultural tourism.
62873.m: Athens was the first European Capital of Culture in 1985.

62874.q: Which development especially boosted short trips to European cities from the 1990s?
a: The building of new cruise ports
The ban on cars in city centres
62874.e: Cheap flights made weekend trips to London, Barcelona or Berlin affordable for many. City breaks are usually short and often last only one to three nights.
62874.m: Low-cost flights made weekend city breaks popular.

62875.q: Why do overnight stay statistics often underestimate city tourism?
a: Day visitors who do not stay overnight are not counted
62875.e: Many visitors leave again on the same day, for example cruise guests or day trippers. They put a strain on the city but do not appear in hotel statistics.
62875.m: Day visitors are missing from overnight stay statistics.

62876.q: In which city does the World Tourism Organization have its headquarters?
62876.e: The organisation has been based in the Spanish capital since 1976. Spain is one of the most important tourism countries in the world.
62876.m: The World Tourism Organization is based in Madrid.

62877.q: Under which name has the World Tourism Organization (UNWTO) been known since 2024?
62877.e: In January 2024 the brand name was changed to “UN Tourism”. The organisation remains a specialised agency of the United Nations.
62877.m: Since 2024 the UNWTO has been called UN Tourism.

62878.q: What kind of organisation is the World Tourism Organization today?
a: A specialised agency of the UN
An association of private travel agencies
A foundation of the hotel industry
62878.e: The organisation was created in 1975 from an association of national tourism organisations. Since 2003 it has been one of the specialised agencies of the United Nations.
62878.m: The World Tourism Organization is a specialised agency of the UN.

62879.q: When is World Tourism Day celebrated every year?
62879.e: It marks the adoption of the organisation's statutes on 27 September 1970. It has been celebrated since 1980.
62879.m: World Tourism Day is on 27 September.

62880.q: According to the World Tourism Organization's definition, who counts as a tourist and not as a day visitor?
a: Someone who stays at least one night at the destination
Someone who travels more than 100 kilometres
62880.e: Travellers who do not stay overnight count as day visitors. Tourists stay at least one night outside their usual environment.
62880.m: A tourist stays at least one night at the destination.

62881.q: Roughly how many international tourist arrivals did the World Tourism Organization count in the record year 2019?
62881.e: In 2019 about 1.46 billion international arrivals were counted. In 2020 they fell by about three quarters because of the Covid pandemic.
62881.m: Before the pandemic there were about one and a half billion international arrivals a year.

62882.q: What does the World Tourism Organization's Global Code of Ethics for Tourism contain?
a: Principles for responsible and sustainable travel
62882.e: The code was adopted in 1999. It is meant to protect the environment, culture and people in the destination countries.
62882.m: The Code of Ethics calls for responsible tourism.

62883.q: What has been new at the top of UN Tourism since the beginning of 2026?
a: For the first time a woman leads the organisation
The organisation no longer has a leader
For the first time a person from Switzerland leads it
The leader is chosen by lot every year
62883.e: Shaikha Al Nowais from the Emirates was elected in 2025 and succeeded Zurab Pololikashvili. She is the first woman at the head of the organisation.
62883.m: Since 2026 UN Tourism has been led by a woman for the first time.

62884.q: How do you calculate a country's tourism balance?
a: Income from foreign guests minus spending by residents abroad
Number of arrivals minus number of departures
Hotel income minus wages in the hospitality industry
62884.e: The tourism balance compares what guests spend in the country with what residents spend on trips abroad. A surplus brings foreign currency into the country.
62884.m: The tourism balance compares travel income and travel spending.

62885.q: Which part of the balance of payments does the tourism balance belong to?
a: The balance of trade in goods
62885.e: Travel counts as a cross-border service. The balance of services is part of the current account.
62885.m: Travel is recorded in the balance of services.

62886.q: How is the spending of American tourists in Switzerland recorded in the Swiss balance of payments?
62886.e: Foreign guests buy Swiss services and bring foreign currency into the country. In economic terms this is like an export.
62886.m: Tourism by foreign guests counts as an export of services.

62887.q: A country earns 18 billion francs from foreign guests, and its residents spend 21 billion abroad. What is the tourism balance?
62887.e: Calculation: 18 minus 21 equals -3. The balance is negative because residents spend more abroad than guests bring into the country.
62887.m: A negative tourism balance occurs when travel spending exceeds travel income.

62888.q: Which country traditionally has one of the largest deficits in its tourism balance in the world?
62888.e: Germans travel abroad a great deal, but the country attracts fewer foreign holidaymakers. Travel spending therefore clearly exceeds income.
62888.m: Germany spends much more on trips abroad than it earns from guests.

62889.q: For which country is the tourism balance especially strongly positive?
62889.e: Spain welcomes tens of millions of foreign guests every year. The income far exceeds what Spaniards spend on travel.
62889.m: Spain makes a large surplus from tourism.

62890.q: How does a strong Swiss franc affect Switzerland's tourism balance?
a: It gets worse, because holidays in Switzerland become more expensive and abroad cheaper
It improves, because more foreign guests come
It stays the same, because exchange rates do not matter
It improves, because Swiss people travel less
62890.e: For foreign guests, prices converted from francs go up. At the same time, trips abroad become cheaper for Swiss people.
62890.m: A strong franc puts pressure on the Swiss tourism balance.

62891.q: Travellers from which country have the highest international tourism spending in the world (as of 2023)?
62891.e: According to the World Tourism Organization, Chinese travellers spent the most on trips abroad in 2023, ahead of the USA. Many countries therefore specifically try to attract guests from China.
62891.m: Travellers from China spend the most in international tourism.

62892.q: Since the second homes initiative, what is the maximum share of second homes a Swiss municipality may have in order to approve new ones?
62892.e: Municipalities with more than 20 per cent second homes may in principle not approve any new ones. This affects many holiday resorts in the Grisons and Valais.
62892.m: Above twenty per cent second homes, no new ones are allowed.

62893.q: Who launched the second homes initiative?
62893.e: The environmentalist Franz Weber campaigned for decades to protect landscapes. His foundation submitted the initiative in 2007.
62893.m: Franz Weber was behind the second homes initiative.

62894.q: What was the result of the 2012 vote on the second homes initiative?
62894.e: On 11 March 2012 about 50.6 per cent of voters said yes. Since 2016 the Second Homes Act has put the initiative into practice.
62894.m: The second homes initiative was accepted very narrowly in 2012.

62895.q: In holiday resorts, what is meant by “cold beds”?
a: Second homes that stand empty for most of the year
Emergency shelters in civil defence bunkers
62895.e: Empty second homes create little value but take up building land and infrastructure. Rented flats and hotels, on the other hand, are called “warm beds”.
62895.m: Cold beds stand empty for almost the whole year.

62896.q: What does the so-called Lex Koller regulate?
a: The purchase of property by people abroad
The level of the tourist tax
62896.e: The federal law restricts people abroad from buying residential property in Switzerland. There are cantonal quotas for holiday homes.
62896.m: The Lex Koller limits property purchases by people abroad.

62897.q: A municipality has 1500 homes, 400 of which are second homes. Under the Second Homes Act, may it in principle approve new second homes?
a: No, the share is about 27 per cent
Yes, the share is about 13 per cent
Yes, the share is about 18 per cent
No, the share is about 40 per cent
62897.e: Calculation: 400 : 1500 = 0.267, so about 27 per cent. That is above the limit of 20 per cent.
62897.m: Above a share of twenty per cent, new second homes are in principle banned.

62898.q: In which city was the conference held in 1884/85 at which European powers set rules for dividing up Africa?
62898.e: The Berlin Conference met from November 1884 to February 1885 in Berlin. It was called by Chancellor Otto von Bismarck.
62898.m: The Berlin Conference of 1884/85 took place in Berlin.

62899.q: Which politician called the Berlin Conference of 1884/85?
62899.e: The German Chancellor Otto von Bismarck invited the participants to Berlin together with France and chaired the conference.
62899.m: Bismarck was the host of the Berlin Conference.

62900.q: Which monarch received the Congo Free State as his personal property as a result of the Berlin Conference?
62900.e: The Congo Free State was recognised as the private property of King Leopold II. Only in 1908 did the Belgian state take over the territory as a colony.
62900.m: The Congo Free State at first belonged personally to King Leopold II.

62901.q: Which principle did the General Act of the Berlin Conference set for new territorial claims on the African coast?
62901.e: A claim only counted if the power actually administered the territory and informed the other signatory powers. This principle of effectiveness speeded up the Scramble for Africa.
62901.m: Under the General Act, what counted was the actual occupation of a territory.

62902.q: Which group was not represented at the Berlin Conference of 1884/85?
62902.e: European states, the USA and the Ottoman Empire took part in the conference. Africans had no voice.
62902.m: Africa was negotiated in Berlin without Africans.

62903.q: Which two African countries were the only ones not under European colonial rule around 1914?
62903.e: Ethiopia fought off an Italian invasion at Adwa in 1896, and Liberia had been independent since 1847. All other areas of Africa were under European control.
62903.m: Ethiopia and Liberia were spared by the Scramble for Africa.

62904.q: Which narrow strip of land in Namibia goes back to a treaty between Germany and Britain in 1890?
62904.e: In the Heligoland-Zanzibar Treaty, German South West Africa received access to the Zambezi. The strip is named after Chancellor Leo von Caprivi.
62904.m: The Caprivi Strip is a leftover of colonial border drawing.

62905.q: Which borders did most African countries take over at independence under the principle of “uti possidetis”?
a: The borders of the former colonies
The borders of the old kingdoms
New borders along the great rivers
62905.e: Uti possidetis means roughly “as you possess”. African and Latin American countries thus took over the colonial administrative borders, even though these often divided peoples.
62905.m: Uti possidetis keeps the old colonial borders.

62906.q: Which organisation declared in Cairo in 1964 that Africa's borders as they existed at independence would be respected?
62906.e: The Organisation of African Unity (OAU), founded in 1963, wanted to prevent border wars with this resolution. Its successor since 2002 has been the African Union.
62906.m: The OAU declared the colonial borders untouchable.

62907.q: Which country was created in 2011 as one of the rare exceptions to Africa's unchanged borders?
62907.e: After an independence referendum, South Sudan separated from Sudan in July 2011. This makes it Africa's youngest country.
62907.m: South Sudan has been independent since 2011.

62908.q: Which court decided the border dispute between Cameroon and Nigeria over the Bakassi Peninsula in 2002?
a: The European Court of Human Rights
The Court of the African Union
62908.e: The International Court of Justice in The Hague is the UN court for disputes between states. It awarded the peninsula to Cameroon, and Nigeria handed it over by 2008.
62908.m: Border disputes between states are decided by the International Court of Justice.

62909.q: Through which high mountain range in northern Kashmir does the border between Pakistan and China run?
62909.e: The border between Pakistan and China runs through the Karakoram, where K2 is also located. In 1963 Pakistan ceded the Shaksgam Valley there to China, which India does not recognise.
62909.m: Pakistan and China share a border in the Karakoram.

62912.q: Which article of the constitution, which gave Jammu and Kashmir special status, did India abolish in August 2019?
62912.e: With the abolition of Article 370 the state lost its autonomy. It was divided into the union territories of Jammu and Kashmir and of Ladakh.

62913.q: Which organisation has monitored the ceasefire in Kashmir with military observers since 1949?
62913.e: The UN observer mission UNMOGIP is one of the oldest missions of the United Nations. Since the Simla Agreement India has considered it unnecessary, but Pakistan has not.
62913.m: In Kashmir the UN has been monitoring the ceasefire since 1949.

62914.q: In which year did the Kargil War between India and Pakistan take place?
62914.e: In 1999 Pakistani fighters occupied heights near Kargil on the Indian side of the Line of Control. It was the first war between the two nuclear powers.
62914.m: The Kargil War took place in 1999.

62915.q: Which treaty of 1960 regulates the use of the rivers in the Kashmir area between India and Pakistan?
62915.e: The Indus Waters Treaty was concluded with the World Bank as mediator. India suspended it in April 2025 after an attack in Pahalgam.
62915.m: The Indus Waters Treaty divides the rivers of the Indus system.

62916.q: What are the two areas of Kashmir administered by Pakistan called?
62916.e: Pakistan administers Azad Kashmir (“free Kashmir”) and northern Gilgit-Baltistan. Ladakh and Jammu are on the Indian side.
62916.m: Gilgit-Baltistan and Azad Kashmir are administered by Pakistan.

62917.q: Which European colonial power withdrew from Western Sahara in 1975/76?
62917.e: Until then the territory was called Spanish Sahara. In the Madrid Accords of 1975 Spain handed over the administration to Morocco and Mauritania.
62917.m: Western Sahara was a Spanish colony.

62918.q: What is the name of the mass demonstration in November 1975 in which about 350,000 Moroccans marched into Western Sahara?
62918.e: King Hassan II called for the Green March to underline Morocco's claim. Green stands for Islam.
62918.m: With the Green March Morocco laid claim to Western Sahara.

62919.q: What is the name of the liberation movement that proclaimed the Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic in 1976?
62919.e: The Polisario Front fights for the independence of the Sahrawis. The republic was proclaimed on 27 February 1976.

62920.q: Which country withdrew from its part of Western Sahara in 1979?
62920.e: After attacks by the Polisario, Mauritania made peace and gave up its share. Morocco then occupied this part as well.
62920.m: Mauritania gave up its claims in 1979.

62921.q: What did Morocco build across Western Sahara in the 1980s?
62921.e: The sand wall (berm), more than 2000 kilometres long, is secured with mines. It separates the area controlled by Morocco from the part controlled by the Polisario.
62921.m: A long sand wall divides Western Sahara.

62922.q: What was the UN mission in Western Sahara originally supposed to organise from 1991?
a: A vote on the future of the territory
62922.e: The MINURSO mission monitors the ceasefire and was supposed to hold a referendum on independence or joining Morocco. This vote has still not taken place.
62922.m: The planned referendum in Western Sahara never took place.

62923.q: Near which town in Algeria have many Sahrawi refugees been living in camps for decades?
62923.e: The refugee camps near Tindouf in south-western Algeria were set up after 1975. Algeria supports the Polisario.
62923.m: Many Sahrawis live in camps near Tindouf.

62924.q: From which country did Cyprus become independent in 1960?
62924.e: Cyprus had been under British administration since 1878 and a crown colony from 1925. Britain, Greece and Turkey became guarantor powers.

62925.q: Which event triggered the Turkish military intervention in Cyprus in July 1974?
62925.e: The Greek military junta supported a coup against President Makarios with the aim of union with Greece. Turkey then occupied the north of the island.
62925.m: A coup led to the division of Cyprus in 1974.

62926.q: What is the UN buffer zone that divides Cyprus called?
62926.e: The name goes back to a line drawn with a green pen on a map of Nicosia in 1963. The buffer zone is monitored by the UN force UNFICYP.
62926.m: The Green Line separates northern and southern Cyprus.

62927.q: Which country is the only one to recognise the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus?
62927.e: The Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus was proclaimed in 1983. The UN condemned the proclamation, and no country apart from Turkey recognises it.

62928.q: Which capital has been divided by a buffer zone since 1974?
62928.e: Nicosia is the capital of the Republic of Cyprus and also the capital of Northern Cyprus. Since 2003 there have been crossing points between the two parts.

62929.q: How did the Greek Cypriots vote on the Annan Plan for reunification in 2004?
a: They were not allowed to vote
62929.e: About three quarters of Greek Cypriots voted no, while most Turkish Cypriots voted yes. The plan therefore failed.
62929.m: The Annan Plan failed in 2004 because of the no vote in the south.

62930.q: Which joint industrial zone of North and South Korea near the demarcation line was closed in 2016?
62930.e: In the Kaesong industrial region, North Korean employees worked for South Korean companies. South Korea stopped the project in 2016 after a North Korean nuclear test.
62930.m: The Kaesong industrial region was a rare joint project of the two Koreas.

62931.q: When was the armistice agreement of the Korean War signed?
62931.e: The agreement ended the fighting, but a peace treaty was never signed. Formally, therefore, there is still no peace today.
62931.m: Since 1953 there has only been a ceasefire in Korea.

62932.q: Roughly how long is the Demilitarised Zone across the Korean Peninsula?
62932.e: The zone stretches from the mouth of the Han River in the west to the east coast. It does not follow the 38th parallel exactly, but the front line of 1953.
62932.m: The DMZ stretches about 250 kilometres across Korea.

62933.q: In which place on the demarcation line was the armistice signed and where do meetings still take place today?
62933.e: Panmunjom is home to the Joint Security Area, where soldiers of both sides face each other. Kim Jong-un and Moon Jae-in met there in 2018.
62933.m: Panmunjom is the negotiating place on the DMZ.

62934.q: Which neutral country, alongside Sweden, has been represented on the supervisory commission at the Korean armistice line since 1953?
62934.e: The Neutral Nations Supervisory Commission monitors compliance with the armistice. Swiss Armed Forces members have been stationed in Panmunjom since 1953.
62934.m: Since 1953 Switzerland has helped monitor the ceasefire in Korea.

62935.q: Why have there been several clashes between North and South Korea in the Yellow Sea?
a: The sea border was not settled in 1953 and is disputed
The largest oilfields in Asia are there
North Korea otherwise has no access to the sea
62935.e: The armistice agreement did not settle the sea border. North Korea does not recognise the Northern Limit Line drawn by the UN side; in 2010 there were clashes at Yeonpyeong.
62935.m: At sea, the border between the Koreas is disputed.

62936.q: Why is the Demilitarised Zone in Korea now considered a valuable natural area?
a: Hardly anyone has entered it for decades
It was replanted as a national park
A strict hunting law applies there
62936.e: Because people have avoided the zone since 1953, rare animals such as cranes have been able to spread. It has become an unintended nature reserve.
62936.m: The DMZ has unintentionally become a refuge for nature.

62937.q: What do the Philippines officially call the part of the South China Sea off their west coast?
62937.e: Since 2012 the Philippines have officially used the name West Philippine Sea for their waters. In this way they underline their claims.
62937.m: Even the names of seas can express political claims.

62938.q: What name does Vietnam use for the South China Sea?
62938.e: In Vietnam the sea is called Biển Đông, meaning East Sea, because it lies east of the country. Vietnam rejects the name “South China”.
62938.m: For Vietnam the South China Sea is the East Sea.

62939.q: Which country brought the arbitration case that rejected China's historic claims in the South China Sea in 2016?
62939.e: The arbitral award of the Permanent Court of Arbitration in The Hague in July 2016 was based on the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea. China does not recognise the ruling.
62939.m: The Philippines won the arbitration case against China in 2016.

62940.q: From which state did China take control of the Paracel Islands after a battle in 1974?
62940.e: In the naval battle for the Paracel Islands, China defeated the navy of South Vietnam. Vietnam still claims the islands today.
62940.m: China has controlled the Paracel Islands since 1974.

62943.q: Why is the South China Sea so important economically?
a: Important shipping routes and raw materials
The largest diamond deposits in the world
The only ice-free port in Asia
The most important source of drinking water
62943.e: A large part of world trade passes through this sea to the Strait of Malacca. In addition, oil and natural gas are thought to be there, and the fishing grounds are rich.
62943.m: The South China Sea is a main artery of world trade.

62944.q: What does the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea call the deep seabed beyond national jurisdiction?
62944.e: The mineral resources of the deep seabed do not belong to any single country. Their mining is managed by the International Seabed Authority, and the profits are meant to benefit everyone.
62944.m: The deep seabed is considered the common heritage of mankind.

62946.q: How many metres are there in a nautical mile?
62946.e: A nautical mile corresponds roughly to one arc minute on a meridian. 200 nautical miles are therefore about 370 kilometres.
62946.m: A nautical mile is 1852 metres long.

62947.q: In which country was the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea signed in 1982?
62947.e: The convention was opened for signature in Montego Bay in Jamaica and came into force in 1994.
62947.m: The Convention on the Law of the Sea comes from Montego Bay.

62948.q: Which major power has still not ratified the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (as of 2025)?
62948.e: In practice the USA follows many of the rules but has not ratified the convention. The main reason was concerns about deep-sea mining.
62948.m: The USA has not joined the Convention on the Law of the Sea.

62949.q: Why is the law of the sea also important for landlocked Switzerland?
a: It has an ocean-going fleet under the Swiss flag
It owns an island in the Atlantic
It has access to the Baltic Sea
It runs a harbour in Genoa
62949.e: Since 1941 ocean-going ships have sailed under the Swiss flag with Basel as their home port. Switzerland ratified the Convention on the Law of the Sea in 2009.
62949.m: Swiss ocean-going ships have Basel as their home port.

62950.q: What can a coastal state apply for if its continental shelf naturally extends more than 200 nautical miles into the sea?
62950.e: If the natural extension of the land reaches further, the shelf can usually be extended up to 350 nautical miles. A UN commission examines such applications.
62950.m: A continental shelf can be extended beyond 200 nautical miles.

62951.q: Which underwater ridge are Russia, Denmark and Canada disputing in the Arctic?
62951.e: All three countries argue that the ridge is an extension of their continental shelf. It runs beneath the North Pole.
62951.m: The Lomonosov Ridge decides who owns the seabed at the North Pole.

62952.q: What did a Russian expedition do at the North Pole in 2007 to draw attention to Russia's claims?
a: It planted a flag on the seabed
It blew up the pack ice
62952.e: A mini-submarine placed a Russian titanium flag at a depth of more than 4000 metres. Legally, this action has no effect.
62952.m: A flag on the seabed does not create a legal claim.

62953.q: What role do organisations of indigenous peoples such as the Inuit Circumpolar Council have in the Arctic Council?
a: They have a say but no vote
They have a right of veto
62953.e: Indigenous organisations are permanent participants in the Arctic Council. They are involved in all discussions but do not take part in decisions; only the eight member states may vote.
62953.m: The Inuit have their own voice in the Arctic Council.

62954.q: Which country operates the Pituffik military base, formerly Thule Air Base, in north-west Greenland?
62954.e: The USA built the base in the early 1950s with Denmark's permission. Today it mainly serves for missile early warning and space surveillance.
62954.m: The USA has its northernmost military base in Greenland.

62955.q: In which marginal sea of the Arctic Ocean do Canada and the USA disagree about the course of the sea border?
62955.e: Canada wants to extend the border along the 141st meridian, while the USA wants a line at right angles to the coast. Oil and natural gas are thought to be in the disputed area.
62955.m: In the Beaufort Sea two close allies are disputing a sea border.

62956.q: Which two countries divided the previously disputed Hans Island between them in 2022?
62956.e: The dispute over the small island between Greenland and Canada became known as the “Whisky War”. Since 2022 a land border has run right across the island.
62956.m: Since 2022 Hans Island has been divided between Canada and Denmark.

62957.q: Which Russian mining settlement is on Svalbard?
62957.e: The Svalbard Treaty of 1920 allows all treaty states to carry out economic activities there. Russia uses this right for coal mining in Barentsburg.
62957.m: Russia mines coal in Barentsburg on Svalbard.

62958.q: Which country has built Africa's largest hydroelectric power station on the Blue Nile, causing tension with Egypt?
62958.e: Ethiopia began building the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam in 2011 and opened it in 2025. Egypt fears that less Nile water will reach it.
62958.m: Ethiopia has built a huge dam on the Nile.

62959.q: On which headwater of the Nile is the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam?
62959.e: The dam lies in western Ethiopia near the border with Sudan. The Blue Nile rises in Lake Tana.
62959.m: The large Ethiopian dam holds back the Blue Nile.

62960.q: In which city do the Blue and White Nile join?
62960.e: In Khartoum, the capital of Sudan, the two headwaters flow together. From here on the river is simply called the Nile.
62960.m: The Blue and White Nile meet in Khartoum.

62961.q: Which two countries divided the Nile water almost entirely between themselves in the Nile Waters Agreement of 1959?
62961.e: Egypt received 55.5 and Sudan 18.5 billion cubic metres a year. The upstream countries such as Ethiopia were not involved and do not recognise the agreement.
62961.m: The 1959 agreement favoured Egypt and Sudan.

62962.q: Which colonial power negotiated a Nile agreement with Egypt in 1929 for its East African territories, giving Egypt a right of veto?
62962.e: Britain assured Egypt that no structures would be built upstream without its consent. The upstream countries that later became independent reject this agreement.
62962.m: The Nile agreement of 1929 dates from colonial times.

62963.q: What is the name of the partnership of the Nile countries founded in 1999?
62963.e: The Nile Basin Initiative is meant to promote shared use of the river. However, Egypt and Sudan reject a framework agreement from 2010.
62963.m: The Nile Basin Initiative wants to bring the Nile countries round one table.

62964.q: What does Egypt mainly fear from the filling of the Ethiopian Nile dam?
a: Less water for farming and drinking
62964.e: Egypt gets about 90 per cent of its fresh water from the Nile. Filling the reservoir quickly could greatly reduce the flow in drought years.
62964.m: For Egypt the Nile is a matter of survival.

62965.q: Which lake is considered the main source of the White Nile?
62965.e: The White Nile leaves Lake Victoria at Jinja in Uganda. Lake Tana in Ethiopia, on the other hand, is the source of the Blue Nile.
62965.m: The White Nile comes from Lake Victoria.

62966.q: In which country do the Euphrates and Tigris rise?
62966.e: Both rivers rise in eastern Anatolia. As the upstream country, Turkey can influence how much water flows to Syria and Iraq.
62966.m: The Euphrates and Tigris come from Turkey.

62967.q: What is the name of the large Turkish irrigation and dam project on the Euphrates and Tigris?
62967.e: The Southeastern Anatolia Project (GAP) includes more than 20 dams and many power stations. Syria and Iraq criticise the falling river flow.
62967.m: With the GAP project Turkey dams the Euphrates and Tigris.

62968.q: Which large Turkish dam on the Euphrates was completed around 1990 and led to a dispute with Syria and Iraq when it was filled?
62968.e: To fill it, Turkey cut off the flow of the Euphrates for about a month in January 1990. Syria and Iraq protested strongly.
62968.m: The Atatürk Dam is the centrepiece of the GAP.

62969.q: Which historic town on the Tigris was largely flooded for the Ilısu Dam?
62969.e: The settlement of Hasankeyf, more than 10,000 years old, disappeared into the reservoir in 2020. Some buildings were moved to a new site beforehand.
62969.m: Hasankeyf disappeared into the Ilısu reservoir.

62970.q: What is the joint river formed by the Euphrates and Tigris before reaching the sea called?
62970.e: The Euphrates and Tigris join in southern Iraq and flow into the Persian Gulf as the Shatt al-Arab. The river forms part of the border between Iraq and Iran.
62970.m: The Euphrates and Tigris end in the Shatt al-Arab.

62971.q: Which region's name means “land between the rivers”?
62971.e: The Greek word Mesopotamia refers to the land between the Euphrates and Tigris. Some of the first civilisations arose there.
62971.m: Mesopotamia lies between the Euphrates and Tigris.

62972.q: Why have Turkey, Syria and Iraq been arguing about the water of the Euphrates for decades?
a: Turkey dams the river upstream of its neighbours
Syria diverts the river into the Mediterranean
Iraq sells the water to the Gulf states
The river dries up completely every year
62972.e: As the upstream country, Turkey can use its dams to decide how much water flows to Syria and Iraq. In 1987 it promised Syria a minimum flow, which the neighbours consider too low.
62972.m: Whoever lies upstream on a river controls the water of those downstream.

62973.q: Which Austrian municipality in Tyrol can only be reached by car through German territory?
62973.e: Jungholz is connected to Austria at only one single point, the summit of the Sorgschrofen. That is why it is called a functional exclave.
62973.m: Jungholz can only be reached via Germany.

62974.q: Which German exclave is completely surrounded by Swiss territory?
62974.e: Büsingen belongs politically to Germany but is completely surrounded by the canton of Schaffhausen. It is part of the Swiss customs area, and you can pay there in francs.
62974.m: Büsingen is a German exclave in Switzerland.

62975.q: What distinguishes an exclave from an enclave?
a: The point of view: from the home country or from the surrounding country
Whether the area is by the sea
62975.e: An area is an exclave from the point of view of its own country and an enclave from the point of view of the surrounding country. Büsingen is therefore both at the same time.
62975.m: Exclave and enclave describe the same area from two points of view.

62976.q: Which country separates the Omani exclave of Musandam from the main territory of Oman?
62976.e: The Musandam Peninsula lies on the Strait of Hormuz. Between it and the rest of Oman lies territory of the United Arab Emirates.
62976.m: Musandam is an exclave of Oman on the Strait of Hormuz.

62977.q: Which two countries exchanged more than 160 enclaves in 2015, getting rid of the most complicated border tangle in the world?
62977.e: Around Cooch Behar there were enclaves within enclaves, even a third-order enclave. Through the border agreement, the inhabitants changed nationality or moved.
62977.m: India and Bangladesh dissolved their enclaves in 2015.

62978.q: In which place does the border between Belgium and the Netherlands run through houses and streets like a patchwork?
62978.e: Baarle consists of the Belgian municipality of Baarle-Hertog and the Dutch Baarle-Nassau, with many enclaves in each other. For some houses, the front door decides which country they belong to.
62978.m: In Baarle, Belgium and the Netherlands alternate in a very small space.

62981.q: Which two countries border the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad on land?
62981.e: Kaliningrad lies on the Baltic Sea between Poland and Lithuania. Since they joined the EU in 2004, the area has been surrounded by the EU.
62981.m: Kaliningrad is enclosed by Poland and Lithuania.

62982.q: At which conference in 1945 was it decided to place the north of East Prussia under the Soviet Union?
62982.e: At Potsdam the victorious powers agreed to hand over Königsberg and the surrounding area. The German population was expelled in the following years.
62982.m: At Potsdam Königsberg was awarded to the Soviet Union.

62983.q: Which Russian fleet has its main base in Kaliningrad Oblast?
62983.e: The Baltic Fleet is stationed in the port of Baltiysk. The port is free of ice all year and therefore strategically valuable.
62983.m: The Baltic Fleet is based in Kaliningrad.

62984.q: Which raw material is mined in Kaliningrad Oblast in quantities found nowhere else in the world?
62984.e: The open-cast mine near Yantarny holds the largest known amber deposits in the world. Most of the amber extracted worldwide comes from there.
62984.m: Kaliningrad is the centre of amber mining.

62985.q: What is the narrow strip of land between Kaliningrad and Belarus on the Polish-Lithuanian border called?
62985.e: The strip, about 65 kilometres long, is the only land connection between the Baltic states and the other NATO countries. Militarily it is considered vulnerable.
62985.m: The Suwałki Gap connects the Baltic states with Poland.

62986.q: Which famous philosopher was born in 1724 in Königsberg, today's Kaliningrad?
62986.e: Kant spent almost his whole life in Königsberg and taught at the university there. Today's university bears his name.

62987.q: Which mathematical problem of 1736 goes back to the city of Königsberg?
62987.e: Leonhard Euler proved that you cannot cross each of the seven bridges exactly once. With this, the mathematician from Basel founded graph theory.
62987.m: Euler from Basel solved the Königsberg bridge problem.

62988.q: What is meant by a stateless person?
a: A person whom no state recognises as a citizen
A person with no fixed address
62988.e: According to the 1954 Convention, a person is stateless if no state considers them a national. Those affected often lack access to school, work and health care.

62989.q: What does the Universal Declaration of Human Rights say about nationality?
a: Everyone has a right to it
Only adults have a right to it
Every state may take it away as it likes
It is not mentioned in it
62989.e: Article 15 says that everyone has the right to a nationality. No one may be arbitrarily deprived of it.
62989.m: The Declaration of Human Rights protects the right to a nationality.

62990.q: Which polar explorer created an identity document for stateless refugees in 1922?
62990.e: As High Commissioner of the League of Nations, Nansen introduced the Nansen passport, first for Russian refugees. He received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1922.
62990.m: The Nansen passport helped stateless refugees.

62991.q: Which Muslim ethnic group in Myanmar has been largely stateless since the citizenship law of 1982?
62991.e: The 1982 law does not recognise the Rohingya as a native ethnic group. They are one of the largest stateless groups in the world.
62991.m: The Rohingya are stateless in Myanmar.

62992.q: Which principle of nationality, which also applies in Switzerland, can lead to statelessness for children of stateless parents?
62992.e: Under the principle of descent (ius sanguinis), a child receives the nationality of its parents. If they are stateless, the child receives none without a special rule.

62993.q: Which UN organisation is responsible for protecting stateless people?
62993.e: The High Commissioner for Refugees is based in Geneva. In 2014 it launched the #IBelong campaign to end statelessness by 2024.
62993.m: The UNHCR in Geneva works for stateless people.

62994.q: In which Baltic state have there been many “non-citizens” since 1991, mostly Russian-speaking residents without nationality?
62994.e: After independence, mainly the descendants of immigrants from the Soviet period did not automatically receive citizenship in Latvia. Something similar applies in Estonia.
62994.m: In Latvia there is a special status for non-citizens.

62995.q: What is the 1961 UN Convention on statelessness mainly meant to prevent?
62995.e: The 1954 Convention regulates the legal status of stateless people, while the 1961 Convention is meant to prevent new statelessness, for example among children.
62995.m: Two UN conventions protect stateless people.

62996.q: Which Chinese city was considered the eastern starting point of the Silk Road?
62996.e: Chang'an, today's Xi'an, was the capital of several dynasties. From here the caravans travelled west through the Hexi Corridor.
62996.m: The Silk Road began in the old imperial city of Chang'an.

62997.q: Which desert did the caravans go around on a northern and a southern route along oases?
62997.e: The Taklamakan in the Tarim Basin was considered almost impossible to cross. So the routes ran along its edge from oasis to oasis, for example via Turpan or Hotan.
62997.m: The caravans went around the Taklamakan on oasis routes.

62998.q: Which Chinese envoy prepared the way for trade with the west through his journeys to Central Asia in the 2nd century BC?
62998.e: Zhang Qian travelled to Central Asia on behalf of the Han emperor Wu. His reports about the lands in the west opened the way for trade and embassies.
62998.m: Zhang Qian is seen as a pioneer of the Silk Road.

62999.q: Which people from the Samarkand area long dominated trade on the Silk Road as middlemen?
62999.e: The Sogdians lived in Sogdiana around Samarkand and Bukhara. Their merchants set up trading colonies as far as China, and Sogdian was an important trade language.
62999.m: The Sogdians were the great traders of the Silk Road.

63000.q: Which epidemic probably also spread to Europe along trade routes from Central Asia in the 14th century?
63000.e: The Black Death reached Europe around 1347 via the Black Sea ports. Long-distance trade routes such as the Silk Road helped it spread.
63000.m: Trade routes spread not only goods but also diseases.

63001.q: How did silkworm breeding reach the Byzantine Empire in the 6th century?
a: An emperor bought it by treaty
63001.e: Under Emperor Justinian, monks smuggled silkworm eggs to Constantinople around 552. With that, China lost its monopoly on making silk.
63001.m: Byzantium broke China's silk monopoly by smuggling.

63002.q: Which development weakened the importance of the land routes of the Silk Road from the 16th century?
a: Direct sea trade between Europeans and Asia
The building of the Suez Canal
The end of silk production in China
63002.e: After the sea route to India was discovered in 1498, European traders could reach Asia directly by ship. Ships carried more goods more cheaply than caravans.
63002.m: The sea route to Asia made the caravan routes less important.

63003.q: What are the two main parts of the New Silk Road?
a: An economic belt on land and a sea route
A pipeline network and a power grid
A canal system and a motorway
63003.e: The “Belt” refers to the economic belt over land, the “Road” to the 21st-century Maritime Silk Road. Both are meant to connect China with Europe, Africa and Asia.
63003.m: The New Silk Road combines land corridors with sea routes.

63005.q: Which development bank, founded in 2015 on China's initiative, has Switzerland as a founding member?
63005.e: The AIIB, based in Beijing, finances infrastructure in Asia. Switzerland is one of the founding members, while the New Development Bank is backed by the BRICS countries.
63005.m: Switzerland is a founding member of the AIIB.

63006.q: Which South-East Asian country has been connected to Kunming since December 2021 by a railway built by China?
63006.e: The railway runs from Kunming to Vientiane, the capital of Laos. Its construction was mostly financed with Chinese loans.
63006.m: With Chinese help, Laos got a modern rail link to China.

63007.q: How long is the Trans-Siberian Railway from Moscow to Vladivostok?
63007.e: The classic route measures 9288 km. It is considered the longest continuous railway line in the world.
63007.m: The Trans-Siberian is more than 9000 kilometres long.

63008.q: Which tsar ordered the building of the Trans-Siberian Railway in 1891?
63008.e: Alexander III proclaimed the building in 1891. His son, the later Tsar Nicholas II, turned the first sod near Vladivostok.
63008.m: The Trans-Siberian was begun under Alexander III.

63009.q: Which obstacle in the east did the Trans-Siberian still have to overcome until 1916 in order to run entirely on Russian soil?
63009.e: Until 1916 part of the traffic ran via the Chinese Eastern Railway through Manchuria. The Amur Bridge near Khabarovsk closed the gap on Russian soil.
63009.m: The Amur Bridge completed the Trans-Siberian in 1916.

63010.q: How was Lake Baikal crossed before the route around the southern shore was finished in 1904?
a: With ferries and, in winter, with tracks on the ice
With a tunnel under the lake
63010.e: Icebreaking ferries carried the trains across the lake. In hard winters, rails were even laid directly on the ice.
63010.m: At Lake Baikal the railway first crossed by ferry and over the ice.

63011.q: What does the obelisk at kilometre 1777 of the Trans-Siberian Railway in the Urals mark?
a: The border between Europe and Asia
The highest point of the line
63011.e: In the Urals the line crosses the conventional border between Europe and Asia. An obelisk reminds travellers of this.
63011.m: In the Urals the Trans-Siberian passes from Europe into Asia.

63012.q: Which railway line branches off the Trans-Siberian at Ulan-Ude and runs via Ulaanbaatar to Beijing?
63012.e: The Trans-Mongolian Railway crosses Mongolia and the Gobi Desert. It connects Russia with China via Ulaanbaatar.
63012.m: A railway runs from the Trans-Siberian across Mongolia to Beijing.

63013.q: What is the name of the railway line running parallel to the north of the Trans-Siberian, built mainly in the 1970s and 1980s?
63013.e: The BAM runs north of Lake Baikal to the Pacific. It was meant to open up mineral resources and lay further from the Chinese border.
63013.m: The BAM is the northern sister of the Trans-Siberian.

63014.q: Which country opened the world's first high-speed railway line in 1964?
63014.e: The Shinkansen started running shortly before the 1964 Olympic Games in Tokyo. At first it ran at up to 210 km/h.
63014.m: Japan began the age of high-speed trains in 1964.

63015.q: Between which cities did the first Shinkansen line, the Tōkaidō Shinkansen, run?
63015.e: The Tōkaidō Shinkansen connects Japan's two largest urban areas. It is still one of the most heavily used high-speed lines in the world.
63015.m: The first Shinkansen ran from Tokyo to Osaka.

63016.q: Which speed record for wheel-on-rail trains did a French TGV set in April 2007?
63016.e: The test train V150 reached 574.8 km/h on the LGV Est line. This is still the record for conventional trains on rails.
63016.m: A TGV travelled at almost 575 km/h in 2007.

63017.q: Which country has by far the longest high-speed rail network in the world?
63017.e: Since 2008 China has built a network of over 40,000 km (as of 2023). That is more than all other countries put together.
63017.m: China has the largest network of high-speed lines.

63018.q: According to the EU definition, what minimum speed must a train reach on new lines to count as a high-speed train?
63018.e: The EU requires at least 250 km/h on new lines. On upgraded existing lines, about 200 km/h is enough.
63018.m: On new lines, high speed starts at 250 km/h.

63019.q: Which type of train reached the speed record for rail vehicles of 603 km/h in Japan in 2015?
